doc.title: Jerry Bergonzi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 7, 2022

title: Coltrane quartet, Pharoah Sanders and Miles groups seen live
summary: He saw the Coltrane quartet at Newport in 1963 and many Miles groups, never saw Coltrane with Pharoah, and calls Coltrane's late music fire and water.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: How about the Pharoah Sanders and the late John Coltrane, that music that was so filled with — I don’t have the word for it — but it was so filled with over-the-top, now I’m getting into where I didn’t want to go, so —

Well you know I saw the Coltrane quartet maybe a half dozen times. And with McCoy, Elvin and Jimmy. And one time in 1963 at the Newport Jazz Festival Roy Haynes was there, and it was funny because Count Basie was in the afternoon, Woody Herman, and Coltrane comes on, it’s dusk, and people are leaving in droves. They just weren’t ready for that type of music. But by the time Pharoah Sanders came in the group I was totally into another kind. I was listening to Miles with Wayne, and I saw that group so many times in all their reincarnations when Jack — when Dave Holland first joined the group, when Chick Corea and Jack DeJohnette — one time I even saw them with Wynton Kelly on piano, Keith Jarrett on organ and Chick Corea on electric piano. Three keyboards.

Another time I saw them with Joe Henderson and Wayne at Lennie’s on the Turnpike. So but when, as I used to see Roland Kirk there and Wynton Kelly Trio and — but I never saw the group with Pharoah play. I saw Pharoah play with his group but I never saw him with John Coltrane. I wish I had.
Well that group, from your four elements, his late recordings, “Ascension” and —
I listened to all the recordings but I never saw them.
Okay. Would you say that he had a preponderance of one of those or two of those elements that you talked about?
Lots of emotion. Yes. That’s for sure.
